Name: regularization_backfire_cifar
Title: When Regularization Backfires: A Controlled Study on CIFAR-10 with a Small CNN
Short Hypothesis: On a fixed small CIFAR-10 subset trained with a fixed ResNet-18 from scratch under an identical modest budget, some standard regularizers (dropout, weight decay, label smoothing, RandAugment) reduce top-1 test accuracy below an unregularized baseline. Pinning the setup reveals exactly which regularizers backfire and by how much.
Related Work: Regularization is applied almost reflexively in low-data deep learning to curb overfitting, but practitioners frequently observe that individual regularizers interact badly with small-sample regimes or specific architectures and can underperform a plain baseline. Prior work studies regularizers largely in isolation and in the large-data regime; comparatively little is reported on clean, fully specified negative results in a fixed small-data setting.
Abstract: DATA LOADING: load CIFAR-10 with torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10(root=os.environ.get('CIFAR_DIR','./data'), train=..., download=True). The machine has internet access, so download=True is fine and the dataset is cached under CIFAR_DIR for reuse across runs. ||| Practitioners reach for dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, and label smoothing whenever data is scarce, assuming these techniques improve generalization. In practice the picture is murkier: some regularizers leave a model worse off than a plain baseline. We isolate when this happens under a fully specified, reproducible protocol designed to run on a single ~4-8GB GPU (e.g. an RTX 3050). We use CIFAR-10 with a FIXED 5,000-image training subset (500 per class, seed 0) and the full 10,000-image test set, and a ResNet-18 trained from scratch (no pretrained weights). We compare a no-regularization baseline against four one-variable-at-a-time conditions: dropout p=0.3, weight decay 5e-4, label smoothing 0.1, and RandAugment. The metric is top-1 test accuracy, reported as mean +/- std over 3 seeds (0,1,2). Training is fixed: SGD, lr=0.1 cosine-decayed, batch size 128 (drop to 64 if GPU memory is tight), 30 epochs, no early stopping, no hyperparameter search. The deliverable is a table of test accuracy per arm and seed plus a bar chart with error bars, identifying which arms fall below baseline and by how much.
Experiments: Dataset: CIFAR-10 via torchvision, root from CIFAR_DIR env (default ./data), download=True. Build a FIXED 5,000-image training subset (500 per class, seed 0); evaluate on the full 10,000-image test set.
Model: torchvision ResNet-18, num_classes=10, trained from scratch (pretrained=False). Only this architecture.
Training budget (identical for every arm): SGD, lr=0.1 cosine decay, momentum 0.9, batch size 128 (or 64 if OOM), 30 epochs, no early stopping, no tuning.
Arms (one variable at a time vs. baseline): (1) baseline, (2) dropout p=0.3, (3) weight decay 5e-4, (4) label smoothing 0.1, (5) RandAugment.
Metric: top-1 test accuracy, mean +/- std over seeds 0,1,2.
Deliverable: table of test accuracy per arm/seed and a bar chart with error bars; identify which arms fall below baseline and by how much.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Results may be specific to ResNet-18 and the 5k CIFAR-10 subset.
With 3 seeds, small differences between arms may not be statistically distinguishable.
A fixed 30-epoch budget may not let every regularizer reach its best accuracy (intentional, but limits strong single-regularizer claims).
